cover.headline: Food delivery plus cash is worth more than the share price. Instamart is the risk you are being paid to take
cover.lead: Swiggy runs India's #2 food-delivery app and the #3 quick-commerce network (Instamart). The stock is at ₹{{P.last|num}}, close to its record low and ~60% below its October-2025 high. The fall came after Instamart's losses widened again in Q2FY27 (₹895 cr) while Blinkit, its larger rival, made a profit. Our honest view is that food delivery is a real, profitable and improving business, and Swiggy holds ~₹13,662 cr of cash. These two alone are worth about what the whole company trades at, so the market values Instamart at less than zero. That is too pessimistic, but Instamart is a distant #2 to Blinkit and may never earn Blinkit-like returns. **We initiate with BUY (high risk) and a sum-of-the-parts target of {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}). Keep the position small: our bear case is {{scen.bear.tp|inr}} ({{scen.bear.upside|chg}}).**

arguments.h: Food delivery is profitable and improving, but losing share
arguments.p: Adjusted EBITDA was ₹341 cr in Q2FY27, 3.4% of order value (GOV), up from 0.9% two years ago. Order value is growing ~18% a year. But Zomato is growing faster (21.5%) and earns 5.5%. Swiggy is a solid #2 that is not closing the gap.

arguments.h: Instamart is a cash drain in a market Blinkit is winning
arguments.p: Instamart lost ₹895 cr in Q2FY27 (−9.7% of GOV); Blinkit made ₹184 cr. Blinkit has 2,751 dark stores to Instamart's 1,240 and grows ~80% a year to Instamart's ~31%. Management says losses peaked this quarter. It also said contribution margin had reached breakeven in Q1, and it slipped back in Q2. We do not take the guidance on trust.

arguments.h: The cash buys time, not victory
arguments.p: Cash and investments are ₹13,662 cr, with no debt other than leases. That covers about four years of losses at the current rate (~₹700 cr a quarter). Swiggy will not need new money soon. But every year of losses uses up value that shareholders already own.

arguments.h: The market already assumes the worst for Instamart
arguments.p: At ₹{{P.last|num}}, market value (~₹48,578 cr) less cash leaves ~₹34,916 cr for all the businesses. That is about 19x our FY28E food EBITDA, with nothing left for Instamart. If even modest value is given to quick commerce, the shares have upside. In the bear case, Instamart burns through the cash.

catalysts: Q3FY27 results (Jan-2027): does the Instamart loss actually fall from the Q2 peak, as management says?
Instamart switches to an inventory (1P) model from mid-Q3FY27: watch contribution margin and working capital.
Food delivery growth against Zomato: does the gap narrow?
A decision on loss-making Toing; brokers want it shut.

sections.title: One app, five businesses: how Swiggy makes money

blocks.p: Swiggy is a consumer app that connects customers with restaurants and stores and delivers the order, usually in 10-40 minutes. It does not cook the food or (for now) own the groceries. It earns a **take rate**: commissions from restaurants and sellers, delivery and platform fees from customers, and advertising. The headline measure of activity is **gross order value (GOV)**, the total value of orders placed. Revenue is the slice of GOV that Swiggy keeps.

blocks.callout: **Why "adjusted" EBITDA?** Swiggy reports segment profit as adjusted EBITDA: it leaves out share-based pay (ESOP) and treats rent as an operating cost. Reported EBITDA does the reverse on rent (accounting rule Ind AS 116 moves it below EBITDA). In FY26 adjusted EBITDA was −₹2,871 cr and reported EBITDA −₹3,245 cr. Chapter 10 walks through the bridge.

sections.title: Twelve years: from a Bengaluru food app to a cash-rich, loss-making platform

blocks.p: Swiggy started delivering food in Bengaluru in August 2014. It raised money privately for a decade, peaking at a US$10.7bn valuation in 2022 before investors marked it down to ~US$5.5bn in the 2023 tech downturn. It listed in November 2024 at ₹390. Since then it has raised ₹10,000 cr more through a QIP (Dec-2025, at ₹375), sold its stake in Rapido (₹2,399 cr) and sold a small distribution unit (Lynks). Each of these changed the numbers, as the table shows.

sections.title: Two markets, one dominant winner: Eternal

blocks.p: **Food delivery** in India is a two-player market: Eternal's Zomato and Swiggy. It became rational and profitable for both from 2023, once discount wars stopped. Zomato is bigger (its share of the two-player market has risen from ~54% in FY22 to ~57-58%), more profitable and growing faster. The market itself grows mid-to-high teens a year, helped by more users in smaller cities and more orders per user.

**Quick commerce** (groceries in 10-20 minutes) is the growth market: ~US$13-14bn of order value in FY26 and forecast at US$30bn by FY28 and US$50-57bn by FY30 (HSBC, Morgan Stanley). It is far more crowded: Blinkit (Eternal), Zepto, Instamart, Flipkart Minutes, BigBasket Now, Amazon Now and JioMart. Scale matters because a dark store is profitable only when it handles enough orders a day. Blinkit is adding ~300 stores a quarter and targets 3,500+ by March 2027.

sections.title: Food delivery: the engine, now earning 3.4% of order value

blocks.p: Food delivery is Swiggy's profit engine. Order value rose from ₹28,784 cr in FY25 to ₹34,592 cr in FY26 (+20%) and adjusted EBITDA from ₹566 cr to ₹1,001 cr. In Q2FY27 GOV was ₹10,054 cr (+17.7%) and margin 3.4%. Contribution margin (profit after delivery and discounts, before fixed costs) is stable at ~7.5-7.8%, so the improvement is coming from spreading fixed costs over more orders.

blocks.p: **Toing** is the wrinkle. It is a separate budget-meals app (now in 50 cities) that Swiggy reports under "platform innovations", not food. It lost ₹162 cr in Q2FY27, almost half of food's profit. Management argues it brings in price-sensitive users; JM Financial and BofA argue it cannibalises Swiggy's own food orders and should be shut. We assume losses shrink from FY28 but do not assume it is closed.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** food delivery deserves a profit multiple, not a loss narrative. We forecast margin of 3.4% / 3.9% / 4.3% of GOV for FY27-29E (management's path is 5%; Zomato is already at 5.5%), giving adjusted EBITDA of {{F.seg.food.adjEbitda.0|num}} / {{F.seg.food.adjEbitda.1|num}} / {{F.seg.food.adjEbitda.2|num}} cr. The honest weakness: Swiggy is a permanent #2 with lower margins, and it is not winning share.

sections.title: Instamart: fast growth, deep losses, and a rival that has already won the scale race

blocks.p: Instamart delivers groceries and household items in ~10 minutes from 1,240 dark stores in 133 cities. Order value grew from ₹14,684 cr in FY25 to ₹28,496 cr in FY26, almost doubling, as Swiggy opened bigger stores and pushed into new cities. The cost was an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹3,511 cr in FY26, more than three times what food delivery earned.

blocks.h: What has to happen for Instamart to break even

blocks.p: Management's own arithmetic: Instamart needs ~4% contribution margin and ~₹30 profit per order, which requires ~2.3x today's scale (₹60,000 cr annualised net order value vs ₹26,400 cr now). At ~30% growth that takes about three years, so adjusted EBITDA breakeven is roughly FY30, not FY28. Guidance for Q3FY27 is contribution of 0 to −1% and ~1pp better EBITDA margin. The move to an inventory model should add ~80bp to contribution and shorten working capital by 8-10 days.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we model losses of {{F.seg.im.adjEbitda.0|num}} / {{F.seg.im.adjEbitda.1|num}} / {{F.seg.im.adjEbitda.2|num}} cr for FY27-29E, i.e. still losing money in FY29. Note that revenue will jump in our forecast (Instamart revenue % of GOV rises from ~14% to ~55%) because the 1P model books the full sale value as revenue. That is an accounting change, not more profit. **Brutal truth:** Blinkit proves quick commerce can be profitable, but only for the leader. Instamart has half the stores, less than half the growth, and needs Blinkit to stay rational to reach breakeven.

sections.title: Out-of-home, supply chain and new bets: small, and mostly about costs

bullets: **Out-of-home (Dineout, events):** GOV ₹4,645 cr in FY26, growing ~40%, just profitable. Management targets ₹20,000-25,000 cr GOV and ~₹1,000 cr EBITDA by FY31. A genuine small positive; we value it at {{dcf.parts.2.value|num}} cr.

**Supply chain & distribution:** a low-margin wholesale business (₹10,935 cr revenue, −₹192 cr EBITDA in FY26) that sells to Instamart's sellers. It will shrink as Instamart buys stock directly. It matters for revenue, not value.

**Platform innovations (Toing, Snacc, Pyng, Crew):** losses jumped from ₹58 cr in Q4FY26 to ₹162 cr in Q2FY27 as Toing scaled. We deduct three years of FY28E losses ({{dcf.parts.4.value|num}} cr) from our valuation.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard vs Eternal
blocks.source: Swiggy and Eternal shareholder letters, broker notes as cited, GAM Research

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Swiggy has a **durable position** in food delivery: it is one of only two national networks, with 2.66 lakh restaurants, 7.5 lakh delivery partners and a brand most urban Indians use. That position is hard to copy, which is why food earns money. But Swiggy has **no advantage over Eternal**, which is bigger, more profitable and growing faster in both food and quick commerce. In quick commerce, Swiggy has **no competitive advantage today**. Its strongest asset is its balance sheet, and cash is not a moat.

sections.title: Revenue is compounding; losses are not shrinking fast enough

blocks.p: Swiggy's revenue grew from ₹2,547 cr in FY21 to ₹23,053 cr in FY26, about 55% a year, and was up 36% year-on-year in Q2FY27 to ₹7,571 cr. But the company has never made an operating profit. The operating loss (EBITDA) was ₹3,235 cr in FY26 and the net loss ₹4,154 cr, larger than in FY24 or FY25, because the quick-commerce build-out (Instamart dark stores) is absorbing everything food delivery earns.

pair.title: Revenue: up 9x in five years
Net loss: bigger in FY26 than in FY24
The quarterly operating-loss margin is narrowing
…but absolute quarterly losses are still ~₹800-900 cr

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the margin trend is genuinely improving (EBITDA margin from −23% to −10% in three years), but because revenue is growing fast, the absolute loss has not fallen. Depreciation has doubled (₹612 cr in FY25 → ₹1,217 cr in FY26) as dark stores are added, so the path from EBITDA breakeven to net profit is longer still.

sections.title: Reported vs adjusted profit: the gap is ESOPs and rent

blocks.p: Swiggy's headline "adjusted EBITDA" is ₹374 cr better than reported EBITDA in FY26. Two items explain it. Share-based pay (₹966 cr) is excluded, which flatters adjusted EBITDA. Rent (₹607 cr) is included as a cost in adjusted EBITDA but moved below EBITDA in reported numbers, which flatters reported EBITDA. Neither number is the full picture: ESOPs are a real cost to shareholders (they are diluted), and rent is a real cash cost.

pair.title: FY26: from adjusted to reported EBITDA
ESOP cost is falling but still large

blocks.p: Two further accounting points: (1) Instamart's move to an inventory model will lift reported revenue sharply from H2FY27 while cutting margins as a % of revenue; compare growth on order value, not revenue. (2) Instamart metrics are disclosed on both GOV and NOV (net of discounts) bases, and third-party reports mix them up; we use the company's letters throughout.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** No sign of aggressive accounting, but large ESOPs, adjusted metrics that exclude them, and a coming change in revenue recognition all make headline numbers harder to read.

sections.title: Cash burn: funded for now, but every quarter costs ~₹700 cr

blocks.p: Swiggy has burned operating cash every year: ₹2,898 cr in FY26 and ₹2,169 cr in FY25. Free cash flow (after capex) was −₹3,809 cr in FY26. The gap has been funded by equity: the November-2024 IPO (₹4,499 cr fresh) and the December-2025 QIP (₹10,000 cr at ₹375), plus the ₹2,399 cr sale of the Rapido stake. "Borrowings" of ~₹2,550 cr are almost entirely lease liabilities for dark stores and offices; there is no bank debt to speak of. Note that ~₹5,000 cr of bank deposits sit inside "other assets" on the balance sheet, so the company's own cash figure (₹15,053 cr at Mar-26) is higher than cash plus investments shown below.

pair.title: Operating cash flow has been negative every year
Equity raised to fund the build-out

exhibit.title: FY26 cash bridge: the QIP and Rapido sale paid for the burn

blocks.callout: **Runway:** cash fell from ₹15,053 cr (Mar-26) to ₹13,662 cr (Sep-26), a burn of ~₹700 cr a quarter. Our forecast has the burn falling to ~₹2,200 cr in FY28 and close to zero in FY29. In our bear case (Instamart losses stay at ~10% of GOV), cash would fall below ₹8,000 cr by FY29 and another raise becomes likely.

sections.title: Ownership: foreign investors exiting, domestic funds absorbing

blocks.p: Swiggy has **no promoter**. At the IPO the largest holders were Prosus (~31%), SoftBank (~8%), Accel (~6%) and Elevation (~8%); current named holdings are not disclosed in our sources. Two things are reshaping the register: **(1) the 49.5% foreign-ownership cap** (approved Aug-2026), which forces foreign holders down so that Swiggy counts as Indian-owned and can hold Instamart inventory; and **(2) the ₹10,000 cr QIP** (Dec-2025), over 80% bought by Indian investors (SBI, HDFC, ICICI Prudential and Kotak mutual funds; also Temasek and GIC).

sections.title: Our forecasts: losses narrow, but profit only arrives in FY29

blocks.p: We build the forecast business by business. Each segment's order value (or revenue) grows at our assumed rate; revenue and adjusted EBITDA are set as a % of it. Group reported EBITDA is the sum of the segments, less ESOP cost, plus rent (moved below EBITDA by accounting rules). Every assumption is listed, with our reasoning, in the Assumptions sheet of the Excel model, which recalculates this report's target price.

blocks.p: Most brokers (Citi, Nomura, Jefferies, UBS) remain Buy on the argument we share: food plus cash is worth more than the market value. HSBC, BofA and Goldman are neutral; Macquarie is Underperform on cash burn. Our food multiple (30x) is at the low end of the 30-40x the street uses; we give Instamart a small positive value (0.2x order value, like Elara) where Nomura and JM give it zero.

sections.title: Valuation: sum of the parts, the street's method, gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}

blocks.p: Brokers value Swiggy **part by part (sum of the parts)**: food delivery on EV/EBITDA two years out (30-40x), Instamart on anything from zero to 0.5x order value or a DCF, plus cash. Only ICICI Securities uses a whole-company DCF. We use the same method; P/E is meaningless while Swiggy loses money. The real debate is the food multiple and what Instamart is worth.

exhibit.title: Target and cross-checks vs the share price

blocks.callout: EV/GOV, the yardstick used for loss-making delivery platforms, gives a value ~10% below our SOTP, so the target is not resting on an aggressive food multiple alone. The swing factor is Instamart: valued at zero (as Nomura and JM do), our target would fall by ~₹25 a share.

blocks.h: Sum of the parts in detail

blocks.p: A loss-making group of businesses cannot be valued on earnings. We value each business separately on our FY28E forecasts (sum of the parts), add the net cash we expect at March 2027, and deduct the cost of the new bets. Every input is live in the SOTP sheet of the Excel model, with Base / Bull / Bear switches.

bullets: **Food delivery:** Brokers value Swiggy food at 30-40x FY28E EBITDA (Anand Rathi 30x, MOFSL 32x, Elara 34x, JM 35x, Nomura and HDFC Sec 40x). Eternal's food business is valued at ~38x; 30x is a ~20% discount for lower margins and share loss.
**Instamart (quick commerce):** Blinkit is valued at ~1.2x GOV by brokers; Instamart at a deep discount as a distant #2. Adjustment = losses from FY28 until breakeven (bear: it never gets there).
**Supply chain & distribution:** Low-margin trading business shrinking as Instamart goes 1P.
**Platform innovations (Toing):** Capitalised cost of new bets: three years of FY28E losses (bull: shut in a year; bear: five years).
**Net cash at end-FY27E (after leases):** Model forecast: cash + investments + deposits − borrowings (incl. lease liabilities) at Mar-27.
**Add back lease liabilities:** Lease liabilities (₹2,451 cr, Mar-26) are dark-store rent obligations; segment EBITDA is after rent, so deducting them again would double count.

cells: Food margin rises to ~4.3% of GOV by FY29 and earns 30x; Instamart losses fall from the Q2FY27 peak but it still loses money in FY29; valued at 0.2x GOV less losses to come.

blocks.callout: **Cross-check: what is the market paying for?** Market value is ~₹48,578 cr. If food, out-of-home, supply chain, new bets and cash are worth what we think (₹72,579 cr), the market is valuing Instamart at about **−₹24,001 cr**, i.e. as a business that will destroy that much value. Put differently, with Instamart at zero, today's price buys the food business at ~19x FY28E EBITDA, against 35-42x that brokers apply to Zomato's food business. That gap is our upside; Instamart's burn is the risk to it.

sections.title: Our honest summary: BUY, but small and staged

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a profitable, improving #2 food-delivery business plus ~₹13,662 cr of cash, at a price that values quick commerce below zero.

**What can go wrong:** Instamart keeps losing ₹3,000 cr+ a year against a dominant, profitable Blinkit; management keeps missing its own guidance; food delivery keeps ceding share to Zomato; Toing keeps leaking cash; gig-worker levies and GST demands add costs. In that world the cash shrinks every quarter and the "food + cash" floor erodes. That is our bear case of {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

bullets: **Rating: BUY (high risk), target {{dcf.tp|inr}}.** Most of the upside comes from the food business being re-valued, not from Instamart winning.
**Position size:** half a normal weight, built in two or three tranches around the next two results.
**Add if:** Instamart's quarterly loss falls below ₹600 cr, contribution margin turns positive, or Toing is shut.
**Exit if:** Instamart losses stay above ₹900 cr for two more quarters, cash falls below ₹10,000 cr, or food growth drops below 15%.

sections.title: Annotated financials
Glossary

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Total value of orders placed by customers, including taxes, fees and tips, before discounts. The basic measure of how much business flows through the app.
Order value after all discounts. Instamart reports both; Blinkit reports NOV.
Revenue as a % of order value: the share Swiggy keeps through commissions, fees and advertising.
Profit on each order after delivery costs and discounts, before fixed costs such as technology and head office.
Swiggy's own profit measure: operating profit before ESOP cost, with rent treated as an operating cost.
Operating profit under accounting rules: includes ESOP cost, excludes rent (moved to depreciation and interest under Ind AS 116).
A small warehouse closed to the public, used only to pack quick-commerce orders.
The platform buys and owns the goods it sells (first party), booking the full sale value as revenue. The marketplace model only earns a fee on others' sales.
Indian-owned and controlled company. Only these may run an inventory e-commerce model; it requires foreign ownership below 50%.
Monthly transacting users: customers who ordered at least once in the month.
Employee stock options. A non-cash cost in the accounts, but it dilutes existing shareholders.
Qualified institutional placement: a share sale to institutional investors.
Sum of the parts: valuing each business separately and adding them up.
Enterprise value (market value less net cash) divided by EBITDA or by order value; used to value businesses that are not yet profitable.
